title: In 1920, a farmer found a 60-ton iron slab in Namibia: Earth's largest intact meteorite is still there today
excerpt: Discovered near Grootfontein more than a century ago, the enormous iron mass has remained at its original site ever since.
content:
Found in 1920 by farmer Jacobus Hermanus Brits, the Hoba meteorite remains exactly where it was discovered, near Grootfontein in northern Namibia. Today, it is recognized as the largest intact meteorite known to exist on Earth.

Made primarily of iron and nickel, Hoba is estimated to weigh around 60 tons and measures roughly 9 feet long by 9 feet wide and 3 feet thick. It covers an area comparable to a small room of about 75 square feet, while its weight is equivalent to that of several dozen cars. Unlike other large meteorites found on Earth, the Hoba meteorite is the largest single, intact meteorite known on the planet’s surface.

An extraordinary piece of space history

No other giant meteorite, including El Chaco in Argentina, Cape York in Greenland or Bacubirito in Mexico, surpasses Hoba as the largest intact meteoritic mass. Hoba has never been fragmented or moved to a museum. Scientists estimate that it fell to Earth less than 80,000 years ago, although the material that makes up the meteorite formed hundreds of millions of years ago in the solar system.

Hoba is classified as an ataxite, a relatively rare type of iron meteorite with a high nickel content. Studying it has helped scientists better understand the composition of primitive metallic asteroids and the processes that shaped the bodies of the solar system.

The meteorite was declared a national monument in 1955 to protect it from damage after visitors began removing pieces as souvenirs.

A major tourist attraction in Namibia

Today, Hoba is one of Namibia’s major geological and tourist attractions, drawing thousands of visitors each year. Because of its enormous weight, the meteorite has never been moved from the site where it landed.

The site has been developed for tourism and includes a small visitor center and a stone amphitheater built around the enormous metal mass, allowing visitors to get a close look at one of Earth’s most remarkable extraterrestrial objects.
